name: Erlitou culture
info: The Erlitou culture was an early Bronze Age society of the Yellow River valley (c. 1750–1500 BCE by radiocarbon dating), named after a palace city in Henan and identified by many scholars, especially in China, with the Xia dynasty.

facts.homeland: The Yellow River valley: Henan and Shanxi, later also Shaanxi and Hubei; the type site at Erlitou in Yanshi, Henan, on the Yi River, a tributary of the Luo.
facts.period: Early estimates c. 1900–1500 BCE; radiocarbon dating since 2007 gives 1750–1500 BCE. The Erlitou site grew in four phases; Phase IV overlaps the Lower Erligang culture (1600–1450 BCE), and in the Upper Erligang phase (1450–1300 BCE) Erlitou shrank to a village.
facts.known: the palace city of Erlitou, with its walled palace complex and courtyards; the earliest large-scale bronze casting in China, in section moulds; the earliest bronze ding and the first bronze dagger-axes; early metal bells; jade ritual blades (zhang) and dagger-axes (ge); the earliest tracks of wheeled vehicles in China; symbols on pottery
facts.sources: Excavations at Erlitou, discovered in 1959 by Xu Xusheng; radiocarbon dating since 2007; the Xia–Shang–Zhou Chronology Project; traditional accounts written down much later, such as the Bamboo Annals and the Records of the Grand Historian. No contemporary written records have been found.

t: Most archaeologists consider the Erlitou culture, centred on a palace city in Henan, the first state-level society in China.
Erlitou was the earliest large-scale bronze-producing culture in China, and the city monopolised the casting of ritual bronze vessels, among them the earliest ding.
Chinese archaeologists generally identify it with the later part of the Xia dynasty, but some Western scholars call this premature, since no contemporary writing has been found to prove the link.
dyk: Tracks of vehicles found near the palace area at Erlitou are the earliest evidence of wheeled wagons in China.
ev: An outburst flood at Jishi Gorge destroys the Lajia site on the upper Yellow River, a flood some authors link to the later Xia flood myth
By radiocarbon dating the Erlitou culture begins, and Erlitou grows quickly into a regional centre of several thousand people
A walled city is built at Yanshi, 6 km northeast of Erlitou, which the Xia–Shang–Zhou Chronology Project takes as the founding of the Shang
In the Upper Erligang phase all the palaces of Erlitou are abandoned and the city shrinks to a village of 30 ha
Xu Xusheng discovers the Erlitou site and suggests it was Bo, the first capital of the Shang
Archaeologists in China begin to identify Erlitou with Zhenxun, the last capital of the Xia
Radiocarbon studies narrow the culture’s dates to 1750–1500 BCE
The Erlitou Site Museum of the Xia Capital, with more than 2,000 objects from the site, opens in Luoyang

sections.origins:
The Erlitou culture was an early Bronze Age society and archaeological culture of the Yellow River valley, named after the site of Erlitou in Yanshi, Henan. Early estimates dated it from about 1900 to 1500 BCE; radiocarbon studies since 2007 have given a narrower span of 1750–1500 BCE. It may have grown out of the matrix of the Longshan culture. First centred on Henan and Shanxi, it later spread to Shaanxi and Hubei.

Its rise followed the decline of the Longshan culture on the North China Plain. A large outburst flood at Jishi Gorge, which destroyed the Lajia site on the upper Yellow River, has been dated to about 1920 BCE, shortly before the rise of the Erlitou culture in the middle Yellow River valley and of the Yueshi culture in Shandong. The authors of that dating suggest that the flood may lie behind the later myth and helped bring about the change of cultures, though no evidence of widespread flooding at that time has yet been found on the North China Plain.

Erlitou was discovered in 1959 by Xu Xusheng. It is the largest site of the culture, with palace buildings and bronze workshops, and most archaeologists consider the Erlitou culture the first state-level society in China.
sections.society:
The city of Erlitou stood on the Yi River, a tributary of the Luo, which flows into the Yellow River. It measured 2.4 by 1.9 km, though flood damage has left only 3 km² of it. Its growth falls into four phases. In Phase I it covered 100 ha and was a fast-growing regional centre of several thousand people, not yet an urban civilisation. Urban life began in Phase II, when it grew to 300 ha and around 11,000 people: a 12-hectare palace area was marked out by four roads, holding Palace 3, three courtyards along a 150-metre axis, and Palace 5, with a bronze foundry controlled by the elite to the south. Tracks of vehicles near the palace are the earliest evidence of wheeled wagons in China.

The city peaked in Phase III, with perhaps 24,000 people. A rammed-earth wall two metres thick enclosed the palaces; Palace 1, the largest, covered 9,600 m², and Palaces 3 and 5 gave way to Palace 2 and Palace 4. In Phase IV the population fell to around 20,000, but building went on, with Palaces 6, 10 and 11. The Luoyang Plain has no copper, so ore had to be brought in, perhaps from the Zhongtiao Mountains of southern Shanxi, where the city probably also obtained its salt.
sections.beliefs:
Ritual at Erlitou is known from its objects and buildings rather than from any text. The palace complex, with its courtyards laid out along a long axis, was the heart of the city, and Erlitou monopolised the making of ritual bronze vessels, including the earliest ding found in China, from its fourth phase. Like other cultures of its time, the Erlitou culture worked jade into ritual objects: ceremonial blades called zhang and ritual dagger-axes, or ge. Three jade ge were found at the Erlitou site beside its bronze ones.

Symbols on pottery from Erlitou sites have prompted speculation about links with early Chinese characters, which appear several centuries later in the same region. No clear connection has been shown, and the symbols are treated as markings or proto-writing.
sections.arts:
The Erlitou culture was the earliest large-scale bronze-producing culture in China. Its casters used a new section-mould process to make ritual vessels and other bronzes. Bronze remains are known from the Qijia and Siba cultures, but Erlitou’s are much more advanced and plentiful: tools, bells, weapons, distinctive animal-faced plaques and more than ten kinds of vessel, a range that shows a diverse and systematic craft. More than 200 bronze objects had been found at the site by 2002.

Erlitou bronzes plainly imitate pottery, with plain surfaces or simple geometric patterns; in the third phase the perforated decoration popular throughout the culture appeared on the bronze jue. Many archetypal Chinese objects are first found at Erlitou sites. The earliest bronze ding, from the fourth phase, are decorated with striped grids. The earliest metal bells, one from Taosi and four from Erlitou, dated to about 2000 BCE, may derive from earlier pottery ones. The first bronze dagger-axe, the ge, appeared at Erlitou, where two were found.

Its builders laid out palaces around courtyards, the largest covering 9,600 m², and enclosed them with a wall of rammed earth.
sections.exchange:
Erlitou drew on a wider region for its materials. The Luoyang Plain has no copper, and the ore may have come from the Zhongtiao Mountains of southern Shanxi, where Erlitou probably obtained salt as well. Its bronze working had forerunners in the Qijia and Siba cultures, whose bronzes are fewer and simpler.

Its end came with the rise of the Erligang culture. Phase IV at Erlitou overlaps the Lower Erligang (1600–1450 BCE), and around 1600 BCE a walled city was built at Yanshi, about 6 km northeast of Erlitou. Production of bronzes and other elite goods at Erlitou stopped at the end of Phase IV, at the same time as the Erligang city of Zhengzhou was established 85 km to the east. There is no evidence of destruction by fire or war, but during the Upper Erligang phase (1450–1300 BCE) all the palaces were abandoned and Erlitou was reduced to a village of 30 ha, still inhabited.
sections.legacy:
A major goal of Chinese archaeology has been to find the capitals of the Xia and Shang dynasties that traditional accounts place in the Yellow River valley. Those accounts, at first oral, were written down much later, in the Bamboo Annals (c. 300 BCE) and the Records of the Grand Historian (1st century BCE), and the Doubting Antiquity School challenged their history, above all for the Xia. Oracle-bone writing proved Yinxu at Anyang the last Shang capital, but no such evidence exists for earlier sites.

Because the Erlitou culture lies in the same area, southern Shanxi and western Henan, and the same period, the early 2nd millennium BCE, as the texts give for the Xia, many scholars, especially in China, see it as the Xia’s material remains and Erlitou as its capital. Xu Xusheng first took the site for Bo, the first Shang capital under King Tang; since the late 1970s Chinese archaeologists have tended to see it as Zhenxun, the last Xia capital, and different authors have matched the Shang overthrow of the Xia to the end of each of its four phases. The Xia–Shang–Zhou Chronology Project called all four phases Xia and the walled city at Yanshi the founding of the Shang. Other scholars, particularly outside China, point to the lack of firm evidence and argue that this historiographical focus unduly limits Chinese archaeology.

summary: The Erlitou culture was an early Bronze Age society of the Yellow River valley, c. 1750–1500 BCE by radiocarbon dating, centred on a palace city at Erlitou in Henan. It was the first large-scale bronze-casting culture in China, and most archaeologists see it as China’s first state-level society. Chinese scholars generally identify it with the Xia dynasty, a link others think unproven without written evidence.

notes: Dates: the article gives “early estimates” of c. 1900–1500 BC and radiocarbon dates since 2007 of 1750–1500 BC. I used -1750 and -1500, and gave both in facts and origins. Phase IV overlaps the Lower Erligang (1600–1450 BC), so the site outlives -1500; the culture’s end is the article’s.

Conflict: the earliest metal bells, four of them from Erlitou, are “dated to about 2000 BC”, before either start date (and the Taosi bell is from a Longshan site). I kept the article’s date; the editor may drop it.

Short article (12 KB): beliefs (about 800 characters) and exchange are short, and society, arts and exchange share some facts (the copper and salt, the palaces), because the article has little else. Nothing filled from memory. Where the article states Xia identifications I named who holds them (Chinese archaeologists, the Chronology Project) and who disputes them (other scholars, particularly outside China).
References: DOIs, S2CIDs and hdl numbers dropped from the copied entries. The article spells the culture “Eridou” once (the copper sentence); I ignored the slip.

Left out: the Erlitou dagger-axe as “purely military” (that is the Longshan article); the claim that the Lajia flood timing is “further evidence” for the Xia identification is given only as the authors’ suggestion.
